lessons.title: Rainwater harvesting techniques: tied ridges, contour bunds, and dams
lessons.body: In dryland Africa, every drop of rain counts. Tied ridges are a simple technique: after ploughing, you make ridges 20-30 cm high and 60-90 cm apart, then tie them with cross-ridges every 2-3 meters to form basins. These basins catch rainwater and hold it long enough to soak into the soil. This can increase yields by 30-50% in dry years. Contour bunds are earth banks built along the contour of a slope, spaced 10-20 meters apart. They slow runoff and let water infiltrate. For small dams, you can dig a farm pond 2-3 meters deep, lined with clay or plastic, to store water for supplemental irrigation. In areas with 500-800 mm annual rainfall, a 10x10 meter pond can collect enough water for 1-2 hectares of sorghum during a dry spell. Always dig ponds at the lowest point of your field and keep them fenced from livestock. Maintenance is key: repair ridges and bunds after each season, and desilt ponds before the rains. These methods are labour-intensive but use local materials and can be done with hand tools like hoes and shovels.

lessons.title: Mulching to conserve soil moisture
lessons.body: Mulching is covering the soil with crop residues, grass, or leaves to reduce evaporation and keep the soil cool. In sorghum and millet fields, you can use previous season's stalks, groundnut haulms, or even dry grass. Spread a layer 5-10 cm thick between plants and along rows. This can reduce water loss by up to 70% and lower soil temperature by 5-10Â°C, which is critical for root growth. Mulching also suppresses weeds and adds organic matter as it decomposes. Do not use mulch from diseased plants. In dry areas, apply mulch right after the first rains when soil is moist. If you have limited residues, prioritise mulching around the base of each plant. You can also use living mulches like cowpea or lablab, which cover the ground and fix nitrogen. Avoid mulching in very wet conditions as it can harbour pests. A simple test: dig 15 cm into mulched and unmulched soil after a week without rainâmulched soil will still be dark and moist. Mulching is cheap, effective, and can be done by any farmer with a hoe and a pile of crop residues.

lessons.title: Supplemental irrigation with buckets, drip kits, or treadle pumps
lessons.body: When rains fail, supplemental irrigation can save your crop. For small plots, a bucket and a cup are enough: pour 1-2 litres of water around each plant every 3-4 days during flowering and grain filling. A drip kit is more efficient: a 20-litre bucket with drip lines can irrigate 50-100 plants, delivering water directly to roots with minimal waste. Treadle pumps are foot-operated and can lift water from shallow wells or rivers to irrigate up to 0.5 hectares. They cost $50-$150 and are easy to maintain. Use irrigation only as a supplementâdo not overwater, as sorghum and millet are drought-tolerant but can rot in waterlogged soil. Irrigate early morning or evening to reduce evaporation. If using a treadle pump, direct water into furrows between rows. For bucket irrigation, make a small basin around each plant to hold water. Prioritise irrigation during the booting and flowering stages, when water stress causes the greatest yield loss. A single supplemental irrigation of 20-30 mm at flowering can increase yields by 20-30%. Always check soil moisture by squeezing a handfulâif it crumbles, it's too dry; if it holds together, it's fine.

lessons.title: Recognizing drought stress stages in sorghum and millet
lessons.body: Drought stress shows in stages. Early stress: leaves roll inward and look greyish-green, especially in the afternoon. This is a sign the plant is conserving water. If you see this, act immediately. Moderate stress: leaves turn yellow at the tips, and lower leaves dry out. Growth slows, and the plant looks stunted. Severe stress: leaves become brown and crispy, stems may crack, and the plant wilts permanently. At this stage, yield loss is 50% or more. Critical stages: for sorghum, the booting stage (when the head is forming inside the stem) and flowering are most sensitive. For millet, flowering and grain filling are critical. If drought hits at these stages, you can lose everything. Check your field daily during dry spells. Dig 10 cm into the soilâif it's dry, you need to act. Also look for 'leaf firing'âbrown edges on leavesâwhich means the plant is pulling water from leaves to survive. Early detection lets you apply mulch, irrigate, or thin plants before it's too late. Keep a simple record of rainfall and stress symptoms to plan for next season.

lessons.title: Emergency measures: reducing plant population during drought
lessons.body: When drought hits and you cannot irrigate, thinning plants can save the crop. Sorghum and millet are naturally tillering, but under severe stress, fewer plants mean each remaining plant gets more water. If you planted 30,000 plants per hectare (spacing 30 cm x 30 cm), during a severe drought you can thin to 15,000 plants per hectare (spacing 60 cm x 30 cm). Do this when plants are 15-20 cm tall, before they compete too much. Pull out the weakest plants, leaving the healthiest. For millet, thin to 10-15 cm between plants. This reduces competition for water and nutrients. Another emergency measure is to remove lower leaves of sorghum to reduce transpirationâbut do not remove more than 2-3 leaves per plant. You can also stop all weeding and let weeds die naturally, as they compete for water. If the drought continues, consider harvesting the crop for fodder rather than grain. Thinning is painful but can mean the difference between a total loss and a half harvest. After thinning, apply mulch to conserve the remaining moisture. Record what you did and how the crop responded for future planning.

lessons.title: Choosing the most drought-tolerant varieties as backup
lessons.body: Not all sorghum and millet are equal in drought tolerance. For sorghum, choose varieties like 'Macia', 'Seredo', 'Kari Mtama 1', or local landraces such as 'Mugudhi' in Tanzania. These mature in 90-120 days and can survive 3-4 weeks without rain. For millet, 'Okashana 1' (Namibia), 'Kombi' (Zimbabwe), and 'Pennisetum glaucum' landraces like 'Babala' are excellent. Always plant at least two varieties: one early-maturing (75-90 days) and one medium (90-120 days) to spread risk. Early varieties escape drought by finishing before the dry spell, while medium varieties yield more if rains are good. Get certified seed from local agrodealers or research stations. If you cannot afford hybrid seed, save seed from your best drought-tolerant plants. Test new varieties on a small plot first. Also consider 'stay-green' varieties that keep leaves green longer under stress. Plant early with the first rains to maximise moisture. In dry areas, choose varieties with good tillering and deep roots. Ask your extension officer for the best varieties for your area. Having the right variety is your cheapest insurance against drought.

quiz.q: What is the main purpose of tied ridges in rainwater harvesting?
options: B) To catch and hold rainwater in basins
C) To drain excess water away
quiz.explanation: Tied ridges create basins that capture rainwater and allow it to infiltrate, reducing runoff.

quiz.q: How far apart should contour bunds be spaced on a slope?
quiz.explanation: Contour bunds are typically spaced 10-20 meters apart to slow runoff effectively.

quiz.q: What is a recommended depth for a small farm pond to store water for supplemental irrigation?
quiz.explanation: A depth of 2-3 meters is practical for small ponds and provides sufficient storage without excessive digging.

quiz.q: Which material is NOT recommended for mulching sorghum fields?
quiz.explanation: Diseased plant residues can spread pathogens to the new crop.

quiz.q: What is the recommended thickness of a mulch layer?
quiz.explanation: A 5-10 cm layer is thick enough to conserve moisture but not so thick that it smothers plants.

quiz.q: How much can mulching reduce water loss from the soil?
quiz.explanation: Mulching can reduce evaporation by up to 70%, significantly conserving soil moisture.

quiz.q: Which supplemental irrigation method is most efficient for small plots?
quiz.explanation: Drip kits deliver water directly to roots with minimal waste, making them highly efficient.

quiz.q: What is the approximate cost of a treadle pump?
quiz.explanation: Treadle pumps are affordable, typically costing between $50 and $150.

quiz.q: When is the most critical stage for supplemental irrigation in sorghum?
quiz.explanation: Water stress during booting and flowering causes the greatest yield loss.

quiz.q: How much water should be applied per plant with bucket irrigation?
quiz.explanation: Applying 1-2 litres per plant every 3-4 days is sufficient for supplemental irrigation.

quiz.q: What is an early sign of drought stress in sorghum and millet?
options: A) Leaves turning brown and crispy
B) Leaves rolling inward and looking greyish-green
quiz.explanation: Leaf rolling and greyish-green colour indicate early drought stress as the plant conserves water.

quiz.q: Which stage is most sensitive to drought in millet?
quiz.explanation: Flowering and grain filling are critical for millet, and drought then causes severe yield loss.

quiz.q: What does 'leaf firing' indicate?
options: B) The plant is pulling water from leaves to survive
C) The plant has a disease
D) The plant needs more fertilizer
quiz.explanation: Leaf firing (brown edges) shows the plant is under severe water stress and is sacrificing leaves.

quiz.q: How deep should you dig to check soil moisture during a dry spell?
quiz.explanation: Digging 10 cm gives a good indication of moisture available to plant roots.

quiz.q: What is a recommended emergency measure during severe drought?
options: B) Thin plants to reduce competition
quiz.explanation: Thinning reduces competition for water, allowing remaining plants to survive.

quiz.q: If you originally planted 30,000 plants per hectare, what is a recommended thinning rate during drought?
quiz.explanation: Thinning to 15,000 plants per hectare (60 cm x 30 cm spacing) reduces water competition.

quiz.q: When is the best time to thin sorghum plants during drought?
quiz.explanation: Thinning at 15-20 cm height is ideal before plants compete too much for water.

quiz.q: How many lower leaves of sorghum can be safely removed during drought?
quiz.explanation: Removing 2-3 lower leaves reduces transpiration without harming the plant too much.

quiz.q: Which sorghum variety is known for drought tolerance?
quiz.explanation: Macia is a drought-tolerant sorghum variety widely grown in Africa.

quiz.q: What is a recommended strategy for choosing varieties as backup?
options: B) Plant two varieties: early and medium maturing
D) Plant varieties from other continents
quiz.explanation: Planting both early and medium maturing varieties spreads risk against drought.

quiz.q: Which millet variety is known for drought tolerance in Namibia?
quiz.explanation: Okashana 1 is a drought-tolerant millet variety released in Namibia.

quiz.q: What does 'stay-green' mean in sorghum varieties?
options: A) Leaves remain green longer under drought
B) Plants stay green all year
quiz.explanation: Stay-green varieties maintain leaf greenness and photosynthesis longer under drought stress.

quiz.q: How can you get drought-tolerant seed if you cannot afford hybrid seed?
options: B) Save seed from best drought-tolerant plants
quiz.explanation: Saving seed from your best performing plants under drought can improve local adaptation.

quiz.q: What is the ideal spacing for sorghum after thinning during drought?
quiz.explanation: Thinning to 60 cm x 30 cm gives remaining plants more soil moisture.

quiz.q: Which of these is NOT a rainwater harvesting technique?
quiz.explanation: Drip irrigation is a supplemental irrigation method, not a rainwater harvesting technique.

quiz.q: What is the main benefit of mulching in dryland farming?
options: B) Reduces evaporation and conserves moisture
quiz.explanation: Mulching reduces evaporation, keeping soil moisture available to plants.

quiz.q: How often should you irrigate with a bucket during a dry spell?
quiz.explanation: Irrigating every 3-4 days provides enough water without waterlogging.

quiz.q: What is a sign of moderate drought stress in sorghum?
options: B) Yellowing leaf tips and lower leaves drying
quiz.explanation: Moderate stress shows as yellowing tips and drying of lower leaves.

quiz.q: Which emergency measure can be taken if drought continues and grain yield is unlikely?
quiz.explanation: Harvesting for fodder can salvage some value if grain production is not possible.

quiz.q: What should you do after thinning plants during drought?
options: A) Apply mulch to conserve moisture
quiz.explanation: Mulching after thinning helps conserve the remaining soil moisture for the surviving plants.
